1qw64ha: Talking about family is one of the first topics in any conversation. To do it you need three tools: the verb **tener**, **possessives**, and **adjectives** that describe.
9iovjj: **Tener** is a very frequent irregular verb. This week you use it for three things: family (**Tengo dos hermanas**), age (**Mi abuela tiene ochenta años**), and some physical features (**Tiene el pelo rizado**, **Tiene los ojos verdes**).
hb5r6q: Watch out for age: in Spanish you don't _be_ an age, you _have_ it. **Tengo treinta años**, not _soy treinta_. To ask: **¿Cuántos años tienes?** (tú) or **¿Cuántos años tiene usted?**
ellglk: In negative sentences and general questions, the noun often goes without an article: **No tengo hijos.** **¿Tienes hermanos?** It's like with _hay_: we are talking about existence, not a specific person.
ov1zmg: The forms of **yo** (tengo) and of **tú, él, ellos** (tienes, tiene, tienen) are irregular; **nosotros** and **vosotros** are regular. With **vos** it's **tenés**.
1u1t3yk: Answer _¿Cuántos años tienes?_ with the number alone (**Veintiséis**) or with the full sentence (**Tengo veintiséis años**). Both are natural.
176mdr7: _Un_ goes with the singular; with the plural use a number or nothing.
1v323qw: For hair and eyes we use **tener**.
1d0atmv: Mi, tu, su, nuestro: whose is it?
1afpzf3: Possessives go before the noun and say whose it is: **mi madre**, **tu primo**, **su hermana**.
624py5: They agree with the thing or person possessed, not with the possessor. That's why one person says **mis padres** (two parents) and two people say **nuestra abuela** (one grandmother, feminine).
gi0e1y: **Mi, tu, su** only change in number (mi/mis). **Nuestro** and **vuestro** change in gender and number: nuestro tío, nuestra tía, nuestros tíos, nuestras tías.
1l2g8gq: **Su** can mean his, her, your (usted), their (ellos, ellas), or your (ustedes). If it's not clear, clarify with **de** + person: _la casa de ella_, _el hermano de usted_.
1luqw3u: Don't confuse **tu** (possessive, no accent mark: _tu hermano_) with **tú** (pronoun, with an accent mark: _¿Tú tienes hermanos?_).
1g0akbs: The possessive **tu** has no accent mark; _tú_ with an accent mark is the pronoun.
1e4untj: To describe appearance and personality you use **ser + adjective**: _Mi tía es alta y simpática._ The adjective agrees in gender and number with the person.
1giwrra: Adjectives in **-o**: four forms (alto, alta, altos, altas). Adjectives in **-e** or in a consonant: one form for masculine and feminine, and plural with -s or -es (inteligente/inteligentes, joven/jóvenes). Adjectives in **-or** add **-a** in the feminine: trabajador → trabajadora.
16r7nir: For a mixed group of men and women, the adjective goes in the **masculine plural**: _Mis abuelos son simpáticos_ (the grandfather and the grandmother).
1r409qg: For hair and eyes, use **tener**: _Tiene el pelo largo y liso._ For a person's hair color you can also use **ser**: _Es rubio_, _Es morena_.
1ci6iue: Regional variation: in Mexico they say **güero/güera** for _rubio/rubia_ and **ojos cafés** for _ojos marrones_; in Argentina and Uruguay, **morocho/morocha** for _moreno/morena_.
1c6mt6m: To avoid sounding negative, soften: **un poco** + negative adjective (_es un poco serio_) and **muy** + positive adjective (_es muy amable_).
6b3glg: Family words almost always have a form in **-o** for men and one in **-a** for women: hermano/hermana, tío/tía, primo/prima, abuelo/abuela. Exceptions: **padre/madre**, **marido/mujer**, **yerno/nuera**.
b00u1m: The **masculine plural** is used for a mixed group: **mis padres** = my father and my mother; **mis hermanos** can be only boys or boys and girls. If they are only girls: **mis hermanas**.
wjp8tg: To explain relationships, use **de**: _La hermana de mi madre es mi tía. El hijo de mi tía es mi primo._
1mkb34r: In everyday conversation you hear **mamá** and **papá**, and in Argentina and Uruguay **mis viejos** (affectionately) for parents. For a married couple: **esposo/esposa** (very common in Latin America) or **marido/mujer** (very common in Spain).
ktpn03: _Parientes_ = relatives (the whole family). _Padres_ = father and mother.

1vxmtbc: C, Z, and S: seseo and distinción
h95yfd: The letter **c** has two sounds. Before **a, o, u** it sounds **[k]**: **ca**sa, **co**sa, **cu**ñado. Before **e, i** it has the same sound as **z**: **ce**na, **ci**nco, **za**pato, a**zu**l.
110nljx: That sound of **ce, ci, za, zo, zu** is pronounced in two ways, and both are correct. In most of Spain the **distinción** is used: a **[θ]** sound, like the English _th_ in _think_, different from the **s**. In Latin America, the Canary Islands, and much of Andalusia the **seseo** is used: **ce, ci, z** sound exactly like **s**.
yt3eyr: With seseo, _casa_ and _caza_ sound the same; with distinción, they're different. Choose one system and be consistent; what matters is **recognizing both**. (In some areas of Andalusia there's also **ceceo**: all the **s** sounds are pronounced as [θ].)
1dvwcd1: The **s** always sounds [s], throughout the Spanish-speaking world, although in many areas of the Caribbean, Andalusia, and the Southern Cone it's aspirated at the end of a syllable: _do**s** primo**s**_ → «doh primoh».
8wrh5c: We write **z** before a, o, u (_zapato, zorro, azul_) and **c** before e, i (_cena, cinco_). That's why plurals change: _lápiz → lápices_, _feliz → felices_, _vez → veces_.
d8x72m: **ca, co, cu** = [k] always: cu-ña-do, Car-los, co-ci-ne-ro. Watch out: the second **c** in _cocinero_ is soft.
12sxakk: Say it twice: once with seseo (Sesilia, sinco) and once with distinción (θeθilia, θinco). Choose yours.
1ylb3bf: With distinción, the tongue comes out a little between the teeth in _Lucía_ and _Zaragoza_. With seseo, all sound [s].
963aot: _Feliz_ → _felices_: the **z** changes to **c** in writing, but the sound is the same.
1xz0myc: All these **s** sounds are [s] in all varieties.
